content: Endometriosis is a condition where tissue similar to the endometrium, which normally lines the uterus, is found outside the uterus. This condition can cause significant pain and infertility. Conventional treatments, such as surgery and hormonal therapies, are associated with undesirable side effects and a high likelihood of recurrence. In China, Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is commonly used to manage endometriosis, and substantial research has been conducted to evaluate its effectiveness in reducing pain, improving fertility, and preventing relapse. This review updates a previous analysis published in 2009 in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness and safety of CHM in alleviating pain and infertility associated with endometriosis. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple English and Chinese electronic databases, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, and the Chinese Biomedical Literature Database, covering studies up to October 31, 2011. Only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with confirmed randomization procedures and laparoscopic diagnosis of endometriosis were included. Comparisons were made between CHM and placebo, CHM and biomedical treatments, different CHM interventions, or CHM combined with biomedical treatments versus biomedical treatments alone. Two Chinese RCTs involving 158 women met the inclusion criteria for this review. Both studies employed adequate methodologies but were of limited quality. Neither trial compared CHM with a placebo. The findings showed no significant difference in symptomatic relief between CHM and gestrinone when administered after laparoscopic surgery (relative risk [RR] 1.04, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.91 to 1.18). Similarly, there was no significant difference in pregnancy rates between the CHM and gestrinone groups (69.6% versus 59.1%; RR 1.18, 95% CI 0.87 to 1.59, based on one RCT). However, CHM administered orally and in combination with a herbal enema demonstrated superior symptomatic relief compared to danazol (RR 5.06, 95% CI 1.28 to 20.05; RR 5.63, 95% CI 1.47 to 21.54, respectively). Additionally, the combination of oral CHM and a CHM enema resulted in a greater reduction in dysmenorrhea pain scores compared to danazol (mean difference [MD] -2.90, 95% CI -4.55 to -1.25). For other symptoms, such as lumbosacral pain, rectal discomfort, or vaginal nodule tenderness, there was no significant difference between CHM and danazol. Notably, all women in both studies experienced some degree of symptom improvement. Furthermore, women taking CHM reported fewer side effects compared to those taking gestrinone or danazol. In conclusion, post-surgical administration of CHM may provide benefits comparable to gestrinone. Oral CHM, particularly when combined with a CHM enema, may offer superior treatment effects compared to danazol, especially in relieving dysmenorrhea. CHM also appears to have a more favorable side effect profile than either gestrinone or danazol. However, further high-quality research is necessary to definitively determine the role of CHM in the treatment of endometriosis.
